items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the emergency tenant protection act of nineteen seventy-four
and the administrative code of the city of New York, in relation to the
regulation of rents
items.lawCode: Amd §10, Emerg Ten Prot Act of 1974; amd §26-511, NYC Ad Cd
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S2845

SPONSOR: KRUEGER
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the emergency tenant protection act of nineteen seven-
ty-four and the administrative code of the city of New York, in relation
to the regulation of rents

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

The purpose of this bill is to prohibit an owner from revoking a rent
stabilized tenant's preferential rent upon the renewal of a lease.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

This bill would prohibit building owners from revoking rent stabilized
tenants' preferential rents upon lease renewal. A building owner could
only terminate a preferential rent, and collect the maximum legal regu-
lated rent for a unit, upon a tenant's vacancy. In addition, such a
vacancy could not be caused by the failure of an owner, or an agent of
the owner, to maintain the housing accommodation in a habitable condi-
tion. This bill does not apply to buildings where all of the units are
rent stabilized solely because of a regulatory agreement with a local
government agency and are deeply affordable due to project-based Section
8 rental assistance.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

The ability of building owners to terminate preferential rents upon
lease renewal has exacerbated the displacement of rent stabilized
tenants from their homes, created tremendous hardship and instability
for tenants, and worsened New York City's affordable housing crisis.
Prior to a change in state law in 2003, a preferential rent offered to a
rent stabilized tenant was permanent for the duration of a tenancy and
could only be revoked upon vacancy. As a result of amendments to the
rent stabilization laws in 2003, owners have also been able to end pref-
erential rents and impose maximum legal regulated rents anytime a
tenant's lease comes up for renewal. This statutory change has put
hundreds of thousands of tenants at risk of sudden and unexpected
substantial rent increases. All too many of these tenants have been
unable to pay the higher rents and been forced to leave their homes.
Countless tenants have also been discouraged from raising concerns about
conditions in their apartments and/or buildings because of fears this
could lead to the termination of their preferential rents.

The number of rent stabilized tenants in New York City and Westchester,
Nassau, and Rockland Counties with preferential rents has grown exponen-
tially over the last two decades. According to data from the State Divi-
sion of Housing and Community Renewal, there were 62 preferential rents
registered in 2000, 89,610 registered in 2002, and 266,279 registered in
2015. In New York City, 251,374 rent stabilized homes (more than 31% of
all occupied stabilized units) had preferential rents registered with
the State Division of Housing and Community Renewal in 2017. While the
percentage of units with preferential rents varies significantly
throughout the New York City, there are zip codes where more than 80k of
rent stabilized tenants have leases with preferential rents. Since
building owners currently can revoke a preferential rent anytime a lease
is up for renewal, these tenants lack the security of tenure available
to all other rent regulated tenants who pay their rent and comply with
their leases.

Additionally, the existing law does not contain a "clean hands" require-
ment to ensure that building owners conduct themselves responsibly when
terminating preferential rents and charging the maximum legal regulated
rent upon vacancy. If a tenant leaves an apartment that is uninhabitable
due unsanitary conditions, lack of heat, hot water, electricity,
repairs, etc., an owner can significantly increase the rent upon the
vacancy of an apartment. As such, the law encourages bad actors to
deprive tenants of a habitable apartment in order to benefit from the
ability to abandon a preferential rent.

In order to stem the displacement crisis in New York City and preserve
the affordable housing stock available to working families and moder-
ate-income residents, the rent regulation laws must be strengthened.
This proposed amendment of the preferential rent provisions is an impor-
tant step in that direction.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

None.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2017-2018: S.6527/A.6285
2015-2016: S.2828-B/A.3809-A
2013-2014: S.1775/A.5473
2011-2012: S.448
2009-2010: S.2251/A.465-A
2007-2008: A.10055-A

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

summary: Prohibits an owner from adjusting the amount of preferential rent, rent charged and paid by the tenant which is less than the legal regulated rent for the housing accommodation, upon the renewal of a lease; only allows the owner to make such adjustments upon a vacancy which is not the result of the failure of the owner to maintain a habitable residence.
